name: Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System

clinicalPearls: The jugular venous pressure is the single most important bedside measurement for estimating volume status; the internal jugular vein is preferred over the external because the latter is valved and not directly in line with the superior vena cava and right atrium.

Using the sternal angle (angle of Louis) as the reference point systematically underestimates central venous pressure, so it is better used to separate normal from elevated CVP than to quantify it; venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are clearly abnormal since the clavicle-to-right-atrium distance is at least 10 cm.

The venous waveform is biphasic in sinus rhythm whereas the carotid pulse is monophasic; the venous pulse is not easily obliterated by palpation and changes with posture and inspiration, helping distinguish it from the arterial pulse.

A cannon a wave occurs with atrioventricular dissociation when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; in a wide-complex tachycardia, cannon a waves identify the rhythm as ventricular in origin. The a wave is absent in atrial fibrillation.

Kussmaul's sign (a rise or lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis but also occurs with restrictive cardiomyopathy, massive pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction, and advanced left ventricular systolic heart failure, and is common after cardiac surgery.

Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid pulse) suggests severe aortic stenosis, whereas a sharp rapidly collapsing carotid upstroke (Corrigan's or water-hammer pulse) points to chronic severe aortic regurgitation.

Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is seen in pericardial tamponade but also occurs with massive pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, severe obstructive lung disease, and tension pneumothorax; it reflects exaggerated interventricular dependence.

Fixed splitting of S2 (a wide A2-P2 interval that does not vary with respiration) is characteristic of a secundum atrial septal defect, while reversed (paradoxical) splitting occurs with left bundle branch block, right ventricular pacing, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and acute myocardial ischemia.

The mitral valve prolapse click-murmur complex moves away from S1 with maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) and closer to S1 on standing, a dynamic behavior that helps distinguish it from other systolic events.

Lower extremity edema with an elevated JVP indicates volume overload (heart failure or constrictive pericarditis), whereas edema without jugular venous hypertension suggests hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), venous insufficiency, or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use.

Janeway lesions (nontender hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles) and Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger/toe pads), along with splinter hemorrhages in the mid-nail bed, are peripheral signs of infective endocarditis.

An ankle-brachial index (ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure) is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality; a >2% finger-to-toe oxygen saturation difference on pulse oximetry performs comparably for detecting lower extremity peripheral arterial disease.
harrison.pathophysiology: The cardiovascular examination derives diagnostic and prognostic information from the mechanical and hemodynamic consequences of cardiac and vascular disease. The jugular venous waveform reflects right atrial pressure dynamics: the a wave is presystolic right atrial contraction, the x descent is atrial relaxation, the c wave is the systolic bulging of the closed tricuspid valve, the v wave is atrial filling during ventricular systole, and the y descent is right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening. Reduced right ventricular compliance accentuates the a wave; tricuspid regurgitation accentuates the v wave with a rapid y descent and progressively 'ventricularizes' the waveform; obstruction to right ventricular inflow (tricuspid stenosis, tamponade) blunts or prolongs the y descent. Arterial pulse contour depends on stroke volume, ejection velocity, vascular compliance, and systemic vascular resistance, so fixed outflow obstruction blunts and delays the upstroke while wide pulse pressure states produce a bounding collapsing pulse. Heart sound intensity reflects valve leaflet excursion and mobility, ventricular contractility, and the PR interval, while the distance between the stethoscope and the cardiac event (obesity, lung disease, effusion) attenuates all sounds. Splitting of S2 depends on the relative timing of aortic and pulmonic valve closure, which is altered by conduction delays, shunts, and outflow obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Aortic stenosis (pulsus parvus et tardus, sustained apex, soft A2)
Aortic regurgitation (water-hammer pulse, wide pulse pressure, low diastolic pressure)
Tricuspid regurgitation (prominent v wave, systolic hepatic pulsations)
Constrictive pericarditis (Kussmaul's sign, prominent rapid y descent, pericardial knock)
Pericardial tamponade (pulsus paradoxus, blunted y descent)
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (bisferiens pulse, triple apical cadence)
Mitral valve prolapse (nonejection click and dynamic murmur)
Aortic coarctation / dissection (interarm or arm-leg blood pressure differential, femoral delay)
infectionMimics: Infective endocarditis presenting with peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes, splinter hemorrhages, splenomegaly, clubbing, Roth-type funduscopic findings)
nonInfectiousMimics: Connective tissue disease syndromes producing thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, ankylosing spondylitis, straight back syndrome) that suggest valvular or aortic disease
Hemochromatosis (bronze skin) as a cause of systolic heart failure
Sarcoidosis (lupus pernio, erythema nodosum) as a cause of dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease
Hereditary lipid disorders (tendon, eruptive, or palmar xanthomas; lipemia retinalis) signaling atherosclerotic risk
Noncardiac causes of dyspnea such as obstructive lung disease (barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing)
additionalInvestigations: Noninvasive imaging (echocardiography, including hand-held ultrasound) to confirm structural cardiac disease
Screening abdominal ultrasound when an abdominal aortic aneurysm is suspected by palpation
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to detect white coat and masked hypertension
Ankle-brachial index measurement for peripheral arterial disease and cardiovascular risk
Funduscopic examination of the microvasculature in atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes, suspected endocarditis, and acute visual change
Allen's test before radial artery instrumentation
Pulse oximetry comparing finger and toe oxygen saturation for lower extremity peripheral arterial disease
redFlags: Markedly elevated JVP that does not pulsate with a dusky cyanotic head and neck, suggesting superior vena cava syndrome
Pulsus paradoxus with elevated JVP and blunted y descent, suggesting pericardial tamponade
An interarm systolic blood pressure difference >10 mmHg or femoral pulse delay, raising concern for aortic dissection or coarctation
Differential cyanosis of the lower extremities with a large patent ductus and pulmonary hypertension (right-to-left shunting)
New peripheral embolic stigmata with fever pointing toward infective endocarditis
Orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia, suggesting autonomic insufficiency
harrison.prognosis: Bedside findings carry independent prognostic weight. In heart failure, an elevated JVP and a third heart sound predict the pulmonary artery wedge pressure and are associated with higher risk of heart failure hospitalization and death; an estimated right atrial pressure >10 mmHg predicted a wedge pressure >22 mmHg with high positive value in advanced heart failure. The ankle-brachial index is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality, and higher ambulatory systolic pressures independently predict cardiovascular events and all-cause death. Pulsus alternans indicates severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and when accompanied by electrocardiographic T-wave alternans the arrhythmic risk appears increased.
pitfalls: Using an inappropriately small blood pressure cuff overestimates pressure, while an oversized cuff underestimates it; the bladder should be about 80% of arm length and 40% of arm circumference.
Examining the carotid upstrokes simultaneously, or before auscultating for a bruit, and applying heavy pressure can precipitate carotid hypersensitivity and syncope in susceptible elderly patients.
A cervical bruit correlates poorly with the degree of carotid stenosis, and its absence does not exclude significant obstruction.
Palpation alone is insufficiently accurate to diagnose an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and sensitivity falls with increasing body size.
Homans' sign is neither sensitive nor specific for deep venous thrombosis.
Arcus senilis lacks specificity as a marker of coronary heart disease risk.

Physician-measured blood pressures tend to be higher than nurse- or self-recorded values, contributing to white coat hypertension; conversely masked hypertension can be missed when clinic pressures are normal despite target organ damage.
Heart and pulse findings can be misleading in low cardiac output states and in stiffened arteries from aging, hypertension, or peripheral arterial disease.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale; specific findings convey severity within individual conditions (e.g., pulsus parvus et tardus and a soft A2 indicate severe aortic stenosis; the A2-opening snap interval in mitral stenosis is inversely proportional to the left atrial-left ventricular gradient; a JVP distance >4.5 cm above the sternal angle at 30 degrees, or any venous pulsation above the clavicle in the sitting position, is abnormal; orthostatic hypotension is a fall in systolic pressure >20 mmHg or diastolic >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).
management: Perform a structured bedside cardiovascular examination of the jugular venous pressure and waveform, arterial pulse character, precordium and heart sounds to direct diagnosis and treatment
Use the jugular venous pressure to assess volume status and guide diuretic therapy and fluid management in heart failure
Interpret arterial pulse abnormalities, acting on pulsus parvus et tardus by evaluating for aortic stenosis and on a collapsing water-hammer pulse by evaluating for aortic regurgitation
Confirm structural findings with echocardiography and targeted further imaging
Track prognostic bedside signs such as a persistently elevated jugular venous pressure and a third heart sound to identify higher-risk patients needing intensified therapy and follow-up
Apply adjunctive bedside assessments including the ankle-brachial index, funduscopy and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring as clinically indicated
Refer to cardiology for confirmed valvular or structural heart disease
